correctness.rationale: For a proposed fort with index sets P,Q, an exterior a_i sees |Q|−1_{i∈Q} selected vertices, and analogously for b_i. A same-shore triple is a fort, but no same-shore singleton or pair is. Thus a minimal fort other than a triple has both side sizes ≤2. A singleton selected on one side forces every outside vertex on the other side to be its matched non-neighbor. The only surviving size possibility is n=3 with one selected vertex on one side and the two complementary indices on the other; this fails the neighbor test at an outside vertex on the singleton side. With two on each side, the test requires identical pairs. The resulting aligned quartet is a fort, and the preceding size tests exclude every proper nonempty subfort. Complementing the minimal fort test yields the displayed ordinary forcing polynomial, whose lowest degree is 2n−4 with C(n,2)(C(n,2)−1) sets. For the fort-cover LP, the constant vector 1/3 is feasible. For each shore, summing the triple inequalities gives total weight at least n/3 by the exact incidence multiplicity C(n−1,2), proving the optimum. Equality forces all triple sums to be one. For n≥4 each pair of weights can be compared by using the same two other vertices in the two triples, forcing equality; for n=3 weight one at a_1 and b_2 and zero elsewhere is also feasible and optimal. For K_{n,n}, the same-side pairs are its minimal forts, giving fractional value n and ordinary value 2n−2. Independent literal adjacency/forcing and subset DP for 3≤n≤7 matched exact fort families, every polynomial coefficient, and the triple incidence LP certificate; fort totals were 5,14,30,55,91 and minimum-set counts 6,30,90,210,420. Replay: python3 /workspace/reproductions/check_fan_crown_skew.py crown. The finite check does not prove the all-order result; the LP uniqueness argument is exact. The frozen checker was inspected, not run, and its Python 3.8 note should be 3.10 or later because it uses int.bit_count().
